questions.question: A wallet has one leader and two asynchronously replicated read replicas. A customer tops up, then immediately makes a purchase whose balance check reads from a replica. What can go wrong, and why?
options: The purchase can be declined because the replica may not yet hold the top-up; asynchronous replication promises convergence, not freshness
The top-up can be lost because asynchronous replicas acknowledge writes before the leader has durably stored them
Nothing, because a replica always redirects a read to the leader when it detects that it is behind
The balance check can see the top-up twice because the two replicas each apply it independently
questions.explanation: Asynchronous replication means a replica may lag behind the leader by any amount, so a read there can return a balance that predates an acknowledged write. Replicas do not acknowledge writes (the leader does), a replica cannot know it is behind without coordination, and applying a write on each replica does not double it.

questions.question: Which single clause separates linearizability from sequential consistency?
options: Linearizability requires every client to see the same total order; sequential consistency allows different orders
Linearizability requires the order to respect real time: an operation that completed before another began must come first
Linearizability applies to multi-object transactions; sequential consistency applies to single registers only
Linearizability requires each client's program order to be respected; sequential consistency does not
questions.explanation: Both models require one total order that respects every client's program order. Linearizability adds the real-time clause, which is what forbids a client from reading a value another client has already overwritten. Neither model is about multi-object transactions; that is serializability.

questions.question: History: P writes 100 then 70; client C reads 70 and then reads 100. Which is the strongest model in the hierarchy that accepts this history?
options: Sequential consistency, because each client's program order is still respected
Causal consistency, because the two writes come from one client and are therefore causally ordered
Eventual consistency, because C has observed a write and then a state from before it, which every stronger model forbids
Linearizability, because both writes completed before C's reads began
questions.explanation: W(70) causally follows W(100) from the same writer, and C has seen W(70). Reading 100 afterwards shows C a state before a write it already observed, which violates monotonic reads, causal, sequential, and linearizable consistency. Only eventual consistency, which promises nothing about reads in progress, accepts it.

questions.question: Two clients P and Q concurrently write a and b to the same register without reading each other. Client C observes a then b; client D observes b then a. Under which models is this history acceptable?
options: Only linearizability, because both writes overlapped in real time and so either order is a valid linearization
Sequential consistency and below, because no client's program order is violated
Causal consistency and below, because the writes are concurrent and may be seen in different orders
None, because two clients disagreeing about the final value is a split-brain failure
questions.explanation: Causal consistency only constrains causally related writes; a and b are concurrent, so different clients may see them in different orders. Sequential consistency and linearizability both require a single total order with one last write, which C and D contradict. Divergence on concurrent writes is expected and is resolved by a conflict rule, not a failure.

questions.question: Which guarantee, and which mechanism, is the cheapest fix for a customer who tops up and then sees the old balance on the next screen?
options: Linearizable reads, by routing every balance read to the leader
Read-your-writes, by having the client carry a version token that a replica must have reached before answering
Causal consistency, by attaching vector clocks to every write and buffering out-of-order writes on replicas
Monotonic writes, by applying each client's writes on every replica in issue order
questions.explanation: The incident is a client not seeing its own write: read-your-writes, a per-session guarantee that costs a version token or a sticky session and no leader round trip. Linearizable reads would also fix it but pay coordination on every read; causal consistency is stronger than needed; monotonic writes is about write order, not visibility.

questions.question: A purchase service reads the balance with a linearizable read from the leader and then issues a debit if the balance is sufficient. Two purchases arrive at the same moment. Is the double-spend prevented?
options: Yes, because a linearizable read guarantees that both services observe the most recent acknowledged debit before deciding
Yes, provided the debit is also written to the leader, since the leader serialises all writes and applies them in order
No, because linearizability constrains only the order of writes and says nothing at all about the value a read returns
No, because both reads can return the same balance before either debit lands; the check and the debit must be one atomic step
questions.explanation: Linearizability says what each read means, not that a read and a later write form one step. Both reads can legitimately return 150 if they both precede both debits, and each debit then succeeds. Preventing the double-spend needs a conditional write or a transaction that makes check-then-debit atomic; the leader serialising writes does not make the preceding reads part of them.
